liebermann.notes: The Parker Chronicle (Anglo-Saxon annals) with a Latin appendix on Lanfranc, and two originally separate quires in one hand of c. 925 with Af–Ine, followed by 11th-century lists of bishops; belonged to Canterbury cathedral. The oldest of all the manuscripts, West Saxon rather than Mercian, but not the exemplar of the others.

wormald.shelfmark: Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MS 173 (the ‘Parker Manuscript’)
wormald.wormald_date: Laws written in the 930s, by two scribes, at about the time they were joined to the Chronicle: after quires 1–3 of the Chronicle (to ‘924’) were finished (palaeographically not after 930) and before quire 4 (annals from ‘925’) was added, probably in the 950s, perhaps before 951 (p. 166). Table 4.1: s. x^med (p. 164). The book was copied (into Otho B.xi) in the early eleventh century (pp. 163, 180).
wormald.wormald_origin: Most probably Winchester by the mid-tenth century (Winchester-centred episcopal data, marks for Ealhswith’s death and Frithestan’s accession), though Dumville’s doubts are acknowledged and a court origin is as possible as a royal abbey; Wormald thinks it does not greatly matter which (pp. 167–71). At Christ Church Canterbury by the later eleventh century and continued there (pp. 167, 180); possibly taken there by Ælfheah on his move from Winchester in 1006, after having it copied (p. 180). Table 4.1: Winchester (s. x^med)/Canterbury (after 1001) (p. 164). Wormald argues these MSS belonged to bishops (p. 181).
wormald.laws: Af–Ine (the combined law-book of Alfred and Ine), ff. 33r–52v (p. 163). Text heavily corrupt: e.g. a line lost by eye-skip at Af 1:2; ‘ceape’ for ‘ceace’ at Ine 37 and 62 (with Ine Rb. 62); Af 8 ‘munuc’ for ‘nunnan’ (pp. 171–2 and nn. 38–40).
wormald.other_contents: Mainly the Parker (A) text of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, kept up from the early 890s to the late eleventh century (to 1093 as the MS now stands), preceding the laws; after the laws, papal and episcopal lists and Sedulius’ Carmen Paschale (some damaged leaves restored in a hand very like Chronicle scribe 1’s; perhaps joined to the MS only c. 1600). The laws form a self-contained two-quire ‘booklet’ in two hands found nowhere else, but quire signatures show they were once the collection’s fourth and fifth quires, directly after Chronicle quires 1–3 (pp. 163–6).
wormald.overview: The Parker Manuscript is above all the oldest Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, and its copy of the Alfred–Ine law-book, made in the 930s by two scribes, was deliberately added to the Chronicle as a continuation of it, as quire signatures and matching page layout show. It was probably at Winchester in the mid-tenth century, close to the West Saxon court, and had reached Christ Church, Canterbury, before the end of the eleventh century. The legal text is far from accurate, and the MS's interest is historical rather than practical: it placed West Saxon law alongside the annals of West Saxon military success.
wormald.liebermann_superseded: Liebermann held that the laws had no original connection with the Chronicle before or after them; Wormald accepts that the booklets had lives of their own but shows from quire signatures and matching page format that the law quires were joined to the Chronicle soon after they were written, in the 930s (p. 166).
wormald.key_quote: “the Parker laws were copied by and for people deeply implicated in the West Saxon dynasty’s audacious attempt to persuade the English at large” (p. 171)
wormald.doubts: GUIDE: the guide (Liebermann) says the laws are in one hand of c. 925; Wormald (p. 163) says two hands, and dates them to the 930s (p. 166, ‘best assigned to the 930s’, checked in image). GUIDE: the guide gives the laws as f. 38–57; Wormald gives ff. 33r–52v (Liebermann’s foliation may differ). The guide’s ‘not the exemplar of the others’ needs care: Wormald notes (p. 174 and n. 44) that Liebermann himself thought the Otho Alfred–Ine copied from E, and Wormald agrees (pp. 173–5). Wormald cites Ker, Catalogue no. 39, and Gesetze I p. xxiv. Table 4.1 date s. x^med checked in image. In the early eleventh century the lists preceded the laws, and by 1600 the Sedulius did (pp. 163–6).
verify_notes: liebermann_superseded: page corrected from 165–7 to 166; wording aligned with Wormald (he grants the booklets had separate lives).
other_contents: clarified that the law quires were the collection’s 4th–5th quires (after Chronicle quires 1–3).
doubts: the ‘not the exemplar’ point reworded — Liebermann himself thought Ot copied from E (p. 174 n. 44); ‘930s’ confirmed in image.

The Parker Manuscript is above all the oldest Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, and its copy of the Alfred–Ine law-book, made in the 930s by two scribes, was deliberately added to the Chronicle as a continuation of it, as quire signatures and matching page layout show. It was probably at Winchester in the mid-tenth century, close to the West Saxon court, and had reached Christ Church, Canterbury, before the end of the eleventh century. The legal text is far from accurate, and the MS's interest is historical rather than practical: it placed West Saxon law alongside the annals of West Saxon military success.

Liebermann held that the laws had no original connection with the Chronicle before or after them; Wormald accepts that the booklets had lives of their own but shows from quire signatures and matching page format that the law quires were joined to the Chronicle soon after they were written, in the 930s (p. 166).
